interactions: Warfarin: no established pharmacokinetic interaction; check the INR within 1-2 weeks of starting riluzole, as after any new long-term medicine.
Atorvastatin: no pharmacokinetic interaction; atorvastatin can also raise transaminases, so interpret LFTs with both drugs in mind.
Alcohol (occasional beer): no change needed; heavy use adds to the risk of transaminase rises.
output.summary: No interaction requires a change to riluzole 50 mg twice daily; check the INR within 1-2 weeks of starting it. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN. Report any febrile illness (check the white cell count for neutropenia).
warnings: Hepatotoxicity: transaminase rises are most common in the first 3 months of treatment.
Neutropenia: rare; check the white cell count in any febrile illness.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles with chronic neurogenic change in the left hand and complex tongue fasciculations, normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block, and normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and subtle motor-cortex low T2 signal (supportive only); no mass, haemorrhage, infarct or demyelinating lesion.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cervical or thoracic cord compression, cord signal abnormality or mass.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 920 U/L (5.3x ULN) on atorvastatin; normal blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP; INR 2.4 within the warfarin target.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 82% predicted, SNIP 74 cmH2O and NIF -68 cmH2O, all normal: baseline for 3-monthly monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion and no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No established riluzole interaction with warfarin or atorvastatin; INR check within 1-2 weeks of starting riluzole; LFTs read with the statin in mind and riluzole stopped if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Warfarin has no established interaction with riluzole, but the INR is checked after any new long-term medicine, and atorvastatin can also raise transaminases.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not stop respiratory monitoring because the baseline values are normal.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive left hand weakness with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs, left Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in bulbar, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Repeat FVC and SNIP about every 3 months and ask at each review about orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness and unrefreshing sleep, referring for NIV assessment when these appear or values fall.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Check the INR within 1-2 weeks of starting riluzole.

Review atorvastatin with the prescriber: with CK 5.3x ULN and muscle symptoms, pause it and recheck CK in 2 to 6 weeks; a fall in CK points to a statin contribution, while the ALS diagnosis rests on the neurogenic EMG and upper motor neuron signs.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs and a left Babinski sign with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical region, with active denervation also in bulbar, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.

CK 920 U/L is 5.3x ULN, higher than usual in ALS: consider a myopathic contributor clinically, including statin myopathy on atorvastatin, while the neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs argues against a primary myopathy.

FVC 82% predicted and SNIP 74 cmH2O are normal and set the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CK 920 U/L is 5.3x ULN, higher than usual in ALS; statin myopathy can contribute, but the neurogenic EMG pattern, fasciculations, preserved sensation and upper motor neuron signs argue against a primary myopathy.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward statin myopathy or a primary myopathy

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +1, complex fasciculation potentials. Orbicularis oris: fasciculations.

Left FDI: fibrillations +3, positive sharp waves +2, large polyphasic MUPs (duration >15ms, amplitude >3mV), reduced recruitment. Left APB: fibrillations +2. Bilateral deltoids: fasciculations +1. Bilateral paraspinals C5-C7: fibrillations +1.
Thoracic paraspinals T6-T8: fibrillations +1. Right intercostal: fasciculations.
Right tibialis anterior: fibrillations +1, fasciculations. Right vastus lateralis: fasciculations.
Median, ulnar, sural, and peroneal sensory responses: NORMAL. Normal latencies, amplitudes, and conduction velocities.

Median motor (left): CMAP amplitude 3.2 mV (reduced; reference >4.5 mV), normal distal latency, normal conduction velocity 54 m/s. No conduction block. Peroneal motor (right): CMAP amplitude 2.8 mV (reduced), normal conduction velocity.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with chronic neurogenic change (large polyphasic motor unit potentials, reduced recruitment) in the left first dorsal interosseous and fasciculation potentials, including complex fasciculations in the tongue. 2. Reduced left median and right peroneal CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 3. Normal sensory conduction studies. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells, consistent with a motor neuron disease.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H is a 58-year-old retired army veteran who presents with a 14-month history of progressive left hand weakness and widespread muscle twitching. He first noticed difficulty gripping his rifle cleaning equipment approximately 14 months ago and initially attributed this to repetitive strain from his prior military service. Over the following months, the weakness became more pronounced, and he began to notice visible muscle twitching in both arms and his right thigh. His wife first noticed the tongue twitching approximately 6 months ago. He sought evaluation after reading about ALS in a veterans health newsletter and became concerned by the similarity of his symptoms. He denies any sensory loss, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or cognitive changes. He has had no recent infections, significant toxic exposures, or workplace chemical exposures. He completed a course of warfarin following a right leg deep vein thrombosis in 2019 and was continued on low-dose anticoagulation given recurrence risk factors. He reports no family history of motor neuron disease. His progression has been relentless without any plateau periods.
